prompt: In the section's landscape analogy for a potential energy surface (PES) with two degrees of freedom, what plays the part of the height of the land?

choices.text: The potential energy of the system
One of the two bond lengths
choices.why: The bond lengths are the position on the ground, the two coordinates. The height above each point is the potential energy for that geometry.

choices.text: The kinetic energy of the atoms
choices.why: A PES gives only potential energy as a function of the atoms' positions. Kinetic energy is not part of the surface.

choices.text: The time since the reaction began
choices.why: A PES has no time axis; it maps geometry to energy. The height is the potential energy of each arrangement of the atoms.

explanation: A PES gives the potential energy of a collection of atoms as a function of their positions. For two coordinates, such as two bond lengths, these are the position on the ground and the energy is the height, so each geometry has its own unique potential energy.

prompt: What does the section call a potential energy surface that depends on only one coordinate?

choices.text: A potential energy curve, or energy profile
An energy contour map
choices.why: A contour map shows two coordinates, with isolines of equal energy. With a single coordinate the surface is a curve, also called an energy profile.

choices.text: A hypersurface
choices.why: Hypersurface describes the many-dimensional case, a PES with many degrees of freedom. With one coordinate it is just a potential energy curve.

choices.text: A saddle point
choices.why: A saddle point is a special point on a surface, a transition state. A one-coordinate surface is called a potential energy curve or energy profile.

explanation: The surface may depend on one or more coordinates. With only one, such as the distance between two atoms, it is called a potential energy curve or energy profile, like the H2 curve in Figure 30.10.1.

prompt: On the potential energy curve for two atoms, what is the energy when the atoms are very far apart, and what does it mean?

choices.text: Zero, meaning no interaction
Its minimum, meaning a stable bond
choices.why: The minimum lies at the bond length, where attraction and repulsion balance. Far apart the atoms don't interact, and the energy is zero.

choices.text: Very high, from strong repulsion
choices.why: Repulsion raises the energy only at very close approach. At large distances the energy is zero, meaning no interaction.

choices.text: Negative, from long-range attraction
choices.why: Attraction lowers the energy at distances of several atomic diameters, not at very large ones. Far apart the energy is zero.

explanation: At large distances the two atoms don't affect each other, and the curve sets that energy to zero. Closer in, attraction lowers the energy; very close, repulsion raises it.

prompt: Two atoms are brought together from far apart. Which describes the forces between them, as the section gives them?

choices.text: Attraction at several atomic diameters, repulsion very close
Repulsion at several atomic diameters, attraction very close
choices.why: This is reversed. Attraction dominates at a few atomic diameters and lowers the energy; at very close approach repulsion makes it rise.

choices.text: Attraction at every distance, growing as they approach
choices.why: Then the energy would keep falling and there would be no minimum. At very close approach the force turns repulsive and the energy rises.

choices.text: Repulsion at every distance, growing as they approach
choices.why: Pure repulsion would give no well and no bond. Attraction dominates at several atomic diameters, which is what makes the minimum.

explanation: At distances of several atomic diameters, attractive forces dominate and the energy falls. At very close approach the force becomes repulsive and the energy rises, and the two effects balance at the minimum of the curve.

prompt: The internuclear distance at the minimum of a diatomic potential energy curve defines the bond length. Why does the section say it is more correctly called the equilibrium bond length?

choices.text: Thermal motion makes the atoms vibrate about it
It is where the energy reaches zero
choices.why: The energy is zero far apart, where there is no interaction. At the minimum the energy is at its lowest, and the atoms vibrate about that distance.

choices.text: It is where the attractive force is greatest
choices.why: At the minimum the attractive and repulsive effects balance. It is 'equilibrium' because the atoms vibrate about this distance rather than sitting at it.

choices.text: It is measured with the molecule in chemical equilibrium
choices.why: The word has nothing to do with chemical equilibrium here. The atoms vibrate about this distance because of thermal motion.

explanation: The bond length is the distance at the energy minimum, where attraction and repulsion balance. Thermal motion keeps the two atoms vibrating about this distance, so it is an equilibrium value rather than a fixed separation.

prompt: Bond X has a deeper potential energy minimum than bond Y, so it is the stronger bond. By the general rule the section gives, how do their bond lengths compare?

choices.text: X is probably shorter than Y
X is probably longer than Y
choices.why: This is the reverse of the rule. The section says that in general the stronger the bond, the smaller the bond length.

choices.text: They must be equal
choices.why: Well depth and bond length are separate features of the curve. In general the stronger bond is the shorter one.

choices.text: Bond strength says nothing about length
choices.why: The section does link them: in general, the stronger the bond, the smaller the bond length.

explanation: The bond length is the distance at the minimum of the curve, and the bond strength is set by how deep the minimum is. The section notes that, in general, the stronger the bond, the smaller the bond length.

prompt: Attractive forces act between all atoms, yet H2 exists as a molecule and Ar2 does not. What condition does the section give for an identifiable molecule?

choices.text: The energy minimum is at least of the order of RT
The curve has any minimum at all
choices.why: Argon atoms attract each other too, so their curve has a shallow minimum. It is too shallow to withstand thermal energy, so Ar2 does not form.

choices.text: The atoms are far enough apart to stop interacting
choices.why: Atoms that do not interact cannot be bonded. A bond needs a well deep enough, at least of the order of RT, to resist thermal disruption.

choices.text: The kinetic energy is larger than the potential energy
choices.why: This is not the condition the section uses. The test is whether the well depth is at least of the order of RT.

explanation: Unless the potential energy minimum is at least of the order of RT, thermal energy breaks the pair apart before it can be an identifiable molecule. H2 passes this test; the weak attraction between argon atoms does not form Ar2, though it gives the van der Waals force that holds liquid and solid argon together.

prompt: The section says a bond exists only if the potential energy minimum is at least of the order of RT. Using R = 8.314 J mol^−1 K^−1, what is RT at 300 K, in kJ mol^−1?
explanation: RT = 8.314 J mol^−1 K^−1 × 300 K = 2494 J mol^−1 = 2.49 kJ mol^−1. A pair of atoms whose well is much shallower than this, like two argon atoms, cannot stay together long enough to count as a molecule.

prompt: Using the section's relations E = V + K and K = −0.5V, what happens to the kinetic energy K of the bonding electrons when a chemical bond forms?

choices.text: It rises by half as much as V falls
It falls by half as much as V falls
choices.why: From K = −0.5V, a fall in V makes K larger, not smaller. The rise in K is half the size of the fall in V.

choices.text: It rises by as much as V falls
choices.why: Then E = V + K would not change and bond formation would not be exothermic. K rises by only half the fall in V.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: K is tied to V by K = −0.5V, so it must change when V does. It rises by half the fall in V.

explanation: If V falls by an amount x, K = −0.5V rises by x/2, and E = V + K falls by x/2. The kinetic energy rises, but the change in potential energy dominates, so bond formation is exothermic (ΔE < 0).

prompt: An electron has potential energy V = −16.0 eV. Using the section's relations K = −0.5V and E = V + K, what is its total energy E, in eV?
explanation: K = −0.5 × (−16.0 eV) = +8.0 eV, so E = −16.0 eV + 8.0 eV = −8.0 eV. The total energy is always half the potential energy, E = 0.5V.

prompt: When a bond forms, the potential energy of the electrons falls by 870 kJ mol^−1. Using K = −0.5V and E = V + K, what is the bond energy, −ΔE, in kJ mol^−1?
explanation: ΔV = −870 kJ mol^−1, so ΔK = −0.5ΔV = +435 kJ mol^−1 and ΔE = ΔV + ΔK = −435 kJ mol^−1. The bond energy, 435 kJ mol^−1, is half the decrease in potential energy, as the section states.

prompt: The section shows a PES for water plotted against O–H bond length and H–O–H angle, with its minimum at 0.0958 nm and 104.5°. What does that minimum correspond to?

choices.text: The optimized molecular structure of water
The transition state for breaking an O–H bond
choices.why: A transition state is a saddle point, not a minimum. The lowest point of the surface is the optimized, stable structure.

choices.text: The geometry where the atoms stop interacting
choices.why: Non-interacting atoms lie far apart, where the energy levels off. The minimum is the most stable geometry, the optimized structure.

choices.text: The highest-energy shape the molecule can take
choices.why: That would be a high point of the surface. The minimum is the lowest energy, the optimized structure of water.

explanation: Finding the minimum of a PES gives the minimum energy shape of a molecule. For water that minimum sits at O–H bond lengths of 0.0958 nm and an H–O–H angle of 104.5°, the optimized structure.

prompt: N atoms need 3N coordinates, but the section gives the dimensionality of a PES as 3N − 6 (non-linear case). What do the 6 removed coordinates describe?

choices.text: Translation and rotation of the whole system
Vibration and rotation of the whole system
choices.why: Vibrations are internal motions, and they are what the PES keeps. The removed 3 + 3 are translation and rotation of the entire system.

choices.text: The positions of the two heaviest atoms
choices.why: No particular atoms are dropped. The energy depends only on relative positions, so the 3 translations and 3 rotations of the whole system are removed.

choices.text: Translation of the system in six directions
choices.why: Translation accounts for only 3 coordinates. The other 3 are rotations of the system, which also leave the energy unchanged.

explanation: A reaction depends only on the relative positions of the atoms, not on where the system is or how it is oriented. Removing translation (3) and rotation (3) leaves 3N − 6 internal coordinates.

prompt: For the reaction H + CH4 → H2 + CH3, how many dimensions does the PES have, using 3N − 6 with N the total number of atoms in all the reactants?
explanation: N counts every atom in the reactants: 1 (H) + 5 (CH4) = 6. Then 3N − 6 = 18 − 6 = 12. Using only the atoms of one reactant, such as CH4 (N = 5), would give 9 and miss the coordinates of the incoming H atom.

prompt: Using 3N − 6, where N is the total number of atoms in all the reactants, how many dimensions does the PES for OH + CH4 → H2O + CH3 have?
explanation: N = 2 (OH) + 5 (CH4) = 7, so 3N − 6 = 21 − 6 = 15. A surface with this many dimensions can't be drawn whole, so only a few coordinates are plotted at a time.

prompt: For H_A + H_B–H_C, 3N − 6 gives three coordinates, the three H–H distances. What does the section fix so the PES can be plotted against just R_AB and R_BC?

choices.text: The collision angle, at 180°
The H_B–H_C distance, at its bond length
choices.why: R_BC is one of the two plotted coordinates, so it can't be fixed. The section fixes the angle at which H_A approaches, 180°.

choices.text: The collision angle, at 90°
choices.why: The section fixes the angle at 180°, a straight-line approach. Fixing the angle removes the third coordinate and leaves R_AB and R_BC.

choices.text: The total energy of the three atoms
choices.why: Fixing the energy would pick out a contour, not remove a coordinate. The section fixes the collision angle at 180°.

explanation: The collision angle between H_A and the H_B–H_C molecule is a third coordinate. Fixing it at 180° leaves the energy as a function of the two distances R_AB and R_BC, which can be drawn as a 3-D surface or a contour map.

prompt: According to the section, when can the energy be written as an analytically derived expression in the atomic positions?

choices.text: For very simple systems, such as H + H2
For any system, given a fast enough computer
choices.why: For complicated systems the energy of each arrangement is often too expensive to compute for a large-scale map. Analytic expressions are for very simple systems.

choices.text: Only for systems with a single atom
choices.why: A single atom has no relative coordinates and no PES to speak of. The section's example of an analytic surface is the three-atom H + H2 system.

choices.text: Only for large molecules with many atoms
choices.why: Large systems are where calculation becomes too expensive. Analytic expressions work for very simple systems, or when approximations are made.

explanation: For very simple systems, or with simplifying approximations, the energy can be written as a function of the atomic positions; H + H2 → H2 + H is described by a function of the three H–H distances. For complicated systems, computing every point is often too expensive to map the surface on a large scale.

prompt: Points on a PES are classified by the first and second derivatives of the energy with respect to position. What are these called?

choices.text: The gradient and the curvature
The curvature and the gradient
choices.why: The order is swapped. The first derivative is the gradient (slope); the second derivative is the curvature.

choices.text: The force and the energy
choices.why: The energy is what is being differentiated, not a derivative of it. The section calls the first and second derivatives the gradient and the curvature.

choices.text: The velocity and the acceleration
choices.why: Those are derivatives with respect to time. These are derivatives of energy with respect to position: the gradient and the curvature.

explanation: The first derivative of the energy with respect to position is the gradient, and the second is the curvature. Points with zero gradient, the stationary points, are the ones with physical meaning.

prompt: Stationary points on a PES have zero gradient. What do the section's two kinds of stationary point correspond to?

choices.text: Minima are stable species; saddle points are transition states
Minima are transition states; saddle points are stable species
choices.why: This is reversed. A stable species sits in an energy minimum, and a transition state sits at a saddle point.

choices.text: Minima are stable species; maxima in every direction are transition states
choices.why: A transition state is a maximum only along the reaction path and a minimum across it. That is a saddle point, the 'pass' between valleys.

choices.text: Minima are reactants only; saddle points are products only
choices.why: Reactants and products both sit in minima, since both are stable species. Saddle points are transition states between them.

explanation: Energy minima correspond to physically stable chemical species, such as reactants and products. Saddle points correspond to transition states, the highest point along the lowest-energy path from reactant to product.

prompt: How does the section define the reaction coordinate on a PES?

choices.text: The lowest-energy pathway from reactant to product
The straight line joining reactant and product
choices.why: A straight line may climb over high ground. The reaction coordinate follows the lowest-energy pathway, through the valleys and over the lowest pass.

choices.text: The highest-energy pathway from reactant to product
choices.why: The highest point on the path is the transition state, but the path itself is the lowest-energy route connecting reactant to product.

choices.text: The distance between the two reacting atoms
choices.why: One distance is a single coordinate, not a path through the surface. The reaction coordinate is the lowest-energy pathway from reactant to product.

explanation: The reaction coordinate is the lowest-energy pathway connecting a reactant to a product. The transition state is the highest-energy point along it, at a saddle point of the surface.

prompt: On the section's hypothetical PES, the reactants sit in a deep well on the right and the products in a shallower well on the left. What does this show about the reaction?

choices.text: It is endothermic: products are higher in energy
It is exothermic: products are higher in energy
choices.why: Products higher in energy than reactants means energy is taken in, so the reaction is endothermic, not exothermic.

choices.text: It is exothermic: reactants are higher in energy
choices.why: The reactants are in the deeper well, so they are lower in energy. That makes the reaction endothermic.

choices.text: It has no barrier, since both are wells
choices.why: Between the wells the path passes over a saddle point, the transition state. The well depths show the reaction is endothermic.

explanation: A deeper well means lower potential energy. Because the reactants (deep well) are lower in energy than the products (shallow well), the reaction is endothermic, and the path between them crosses the saddle point labeled 2.

prompt: The section's hypothetical PES has two saddle points: point 2 on the reaction path, and point 1 at higher energy. What does point 1 represent?

choices.text: The transition state of an alternative reaction
The transition state of the main reaction
choices.why: That is point 2, on the minimum energy pathway. Point 1 is a higher saddle point belonging to another reaction possible for these chemicals.

choices.text: A stable intermediate between the wells
choices.why: Stable species sit at minima, not saddle points. Point 1 is a saddle point, the transition state for an alternative reaction.

choices.text: The products of the main reaction
choices.why: The products sit in the shallower well on the left. Point 1 is a higher saddle point, the transition state for another possible reaction.

explanation: Every saddle point is a transition state. Point 2 is the one on the minimum energy pathway from reactants to products; point 1, higher in energy, is the transition state for an alternative reaction of the same set of chemicals.

prompt: For H_A + H_B–H_C → H_A–H_B + H_C with the particles far apart, which potential energy curves describe the system at the start and at the end?

choices.text: H_B–H_C at the start, H_A–H_B at the end
H_A–H_B at the start, H_B–H_C at the end
choices.why: This is reversed. H_B and H_C start bonded and H_A starts far away; at the end H_A and H_B are bonded and H_C has left.

choices.text: H_A–H_C at the start, H_A–H_B at the end
choices.why: H_A and H_C are never bonded in this reaction. It starts as the H_B–H_C molecule and ends as the H_A–H_B molecule.

choices.text: No curve: far apart, the energy is constant
choices.why: Only the far-off atom has no interaction. The bonded pair still has its own potential energy curve, H_B–H_C at the start and H_A–H_B at the end.

explanation: While H_A is far away, the energy depends only on R_BC and follows the H_B–H_C curve. Once H_C has moved far away, it follows the H_A–H_B curve. Both curves look like the H2 curve of Figure 30.10.1.

prompt: Why are the PES and contour map for H_A + H_B–H_C → H_A–H_B + H_C symmetrical?

choices.text: The products are equivalent to the reactants
The collision angle was fixed at 180°
choices.why: Fixing the angle lets the surface be drawn in R_AB and R_BC, but it doesn't make it symmetric. The symmetry comes from products equivalent to reactants.

choices.text: The reaction has no energy barrier
choices.why: The reaction does pass over a saddle point, the transition state. The map is symmetric because an H atom and an H2 molecule are on both sides.

choices.text: R_AB and R_BC are always equal
choices.why: They are equal only along the line through the transition state. The whole map is symmetric because the products are the same species as the reactants.

explanation: The exchange swaps one H atom for another, so it begins and ends with an H atom and an H2 molecule. Because the products are equivalent to the reactants, the energy changes look the same from either side, and the map is symmetrical.

prompt: For H_A + H_B–H_C, one path holds R_BC constant while H_A approaches and R_AB decreases. What does the section say happens to the potential energy along it?

choices.text: It keeps increasing as H_A moves closer
It keeps decreasing as H_A moves closer
choices.why: Pushing H_A in while H_B–H_C stays at its bond length crowds the atoms together. The energy rises continually along this path.

choices.text: It stays constant until the products form
choices.why: Once H_A gets close, the particles interact and the energy changes. With R_BC held fixed, it rises continually.

choices.text: It follows the minimum energy pathway
choices.why: The minimum energy path lets R_BC stretch as R_AB shrinks. Holding R_BC fixed leads to a continually increasing energy.

explanation: This is pathway 1: with R_BC fixed, the energy rises continually as H_A gets closer, until the new H_A–H_B molecule forms and H_C breaks away. It is a costlier route than the minimum energy pathway.

prompt: In one path for H_A + H_B–H_C, the H_B–H_C bond stretches while H_A is still relatively far away. Why does the section call this path unlikely?

choices.text: Stretching the bond first takes a lot of potential energy
It has a lower barrier than the minimum energy path
choices.why: A lower barrier would make it more likely, not less. Stretching H_B–H_C before H_A's attraction helps costs a great deal of energy.

choices.text: H_A repels the H_B–H_C molecule from afar
choices.why: The section's reason is the cost of stretching the bond on its own. Without H_A's attraction nearby, lengthening H_B–H_C needs a lot of energy.

choices.text: It leads to a different set of products
choices.why: It ends with the same products, H_A–H_B + H_C. It is unlikely because stretching the bond before H_A can help costs a great deal of energy.

explanation: This is pathway 2. Lengthening the H_B–H_C bond before the attractive force from H_A can assist requires a great deal of potential energy, so the system is unlikely to take this route.

prompt: Along the minimum energy pathway for H_A + H_B–H_C, the system passes a saddle point, the transition state. Which statement about it is true, according to the section?

choices.text: It is equally poised to return to reactants or form products
It is the lowest energy point on the reaction path
choices.why: The lowest points on the path are the reactant and product wells. The transition state is the highest point on the minimum energy path.

choices.text: It is the highest barrier among the possible paths
choices.why: Its local maximum is the lowest barrier separating reactants from products, which is why this path is the most likely.

choices.text: Once reached, the system always goes on to products
choices.why: At the transition state the system can as easily go back. The section describes it as equally poised to return to reactants or form products.

explanation: On pathway 3 the system still crosses a maximum at the saddle point, but it is the lowest barrier between reactants and products. The transition state structure there is equally poised to go back to reactants or on to products, and pathway 3 is the one most likely followed in a successful reaction.

prompt: The section's contour maps for H_A + H_B–H_C include collisions with slow-moving H_B–H_C molecules that fail to react. Why do they fail?

choices.text: Too little kinetic energy to escape the well
The molecule was vibrating
choices.why: A vibrating H_B–H_C molecule can react successfully, giving a vibrating H_A–H_B. Failure comes from too little kinetic energy, vibrating or not.

choices.text: The molecule was not vibrating
choices.why: Unsuccessful collisions are shown for both a vibrating and a non-vibrating molecule. What they share is too little kinetic energy to leave the well.

choices.text: H_A approached along the minimum energy path
choices.why: Following the minimum energy path is what leads to a successful exchange. The failures come from too little kinetic energy to escape the well.

explanation: Figure 30.10.6 shows successful exchanges along the minimum energy path and for a vibrating H_B–H_C molecule. In the failed cases, vibrating or not, the slow-moving molecule has too little kinetic energy to escape the potential energy well, so no exchange occurs.

prompt: To map the PES for F + D2 → DF + D, the section labels the deuterium atoms D_A and D_B. Which two distances does it use?

choices.text: F to D_A, and D_A to D_B
F to D_A, and F to D_B
choices.why: These leave out the D–D bond that must break. The section uses the F to D_A distance R_(DA F) and the D2 bond length R_(DA DB).

choices.text: D_A to D_B only
choices.why: One distance gives a curve, not a map. The F atom's approach matters too, so the section also uses R_(DA F).

choices.text: F to the center of D2, and the collision angle
choices.why: The section does not use those coordinates. It uses the F to D_A distance R_(DA F) and the D_A to D_B distance R_(DA DB).

explanation: The F atom bonds to D_A while the D_A–D_B bond breaks. So the energy is mapped against R_(DA F), which shrinks as DF forms, and R_(DA DB), which grows as D_B leaves.

prompt: The section gives the potential energy difference between reactants and products of F + D2 → DF + D as D_e(D2) − D_e(DF). Taking D_e(D2) = 455 kJ mol^−1 and D_e(DF) = 590 kJ mol^−1 as illustrative values, what is this difference, in kJ mol^−1?
explanation: D_e(D2) − D_e(DF) = 455 kJ mol^−1 − 590 kJ mol^−1 = −135 kJ mol^−1. The products sit 135 kJ mol^−1 lower than the reactants because the DF well is deeper, and they are reached over a small barrier of about 6 kJ mol^−1 at the transition state.
